source_text: γὰρ ἄν τις καὶ ἐπ' αὐτοῖς καθάπερ ἀμέλει καὶ ἐπὶ τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις. «Μαρτυρῶ γὰρ αὐτοῖς, ὅτι ζῆλον Θεοῦ ἔχουσιν, ἀλλ' οὐ κατ' ἐπίγνωσιν.» Οἰόμενοι γὰρ ὀρθοεπεῖς εἶναι καὶ σοφοὶ, λελήθασι σφᾶς αὐτοὺς οἱ δείλαιοι, καὶ τοῖς τῆς ἀληθείας μαχόμενοι δόγμασι, καὶ ζήλῳ πεπλασμένῳ κατακεκρατημένοι, τῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ δόξῃ συναγορεύειν οἴονται, τοῖς ὀρθοποδοῦσιν ἀντιταττόμενοι. Μωαβῖται δέ γε, τοῦτ' ἔστι, τὰ Ἑλλήνων στίφη, γυμνῶς καὶ ἀναφανδὸν, καὶ ὑποστολῆς ἁπάσης δίχα, τῇ θείᾳ μάχονται δόξῃ. Τοιγάρτοι φορτικωτέραν ἐπήρτησέ πως τὴν δίκην αὐτοῖς ὁ νόμος. Πλὴν ἄμφω τῶν ἱερῶν ἀπόπεμπτοι περιβόλων, ὡς βέβηλοί τε καὶ θεομισεῖς. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Χρῆμα δὴ οὖν οὐκ ἀζήμιον, ὅσον ἧκεν εἰς μολυσμοὺς, τὸ ὀθνείοις τισὶ καὶ ἑτερογνώμοσι, κἂν γοῦν εἰς λόγους ἰέναι φιλεῖν. {ΚΥΡ.} Συνίης εὖ μάλα. Τοιγάρτοι καὶ ὁ νόμος τοὺς ἐκνενιμμένους καὶ καθαροὺς, καὶ οἰκείους ἤδη Θεῷ, διὰ τοῦτο τῆς ἐκείνων βδελυρίας ἀποτειχίζει λέγων· «Καὶ ἔσται ἐν τῷ εἰσαγαγεῖν σε Κύριον τὸν Θεόν σου εἰς τὴν γῆν εἰς ἣν εἰσπορεύῃ ἐκεῖ κληρονομῆσαι αὐτὴν, καὶ ἐξαρεῖς ἔθνη μεγάλα, καὶ πολλὰ, καὶ ἰσχυρὰ ἀπὸ προσώπου σου, τὸν Χετταῖον, καὶ τὸν Γεργεσαῖον, καὶ τὸν Ἀμοῤῥαῖον, καὶ τὸν Χαναναῖον, καὶ τὸν Φερεζαῖον, καὶ τὸν Εὐαῖον, καὶ τὸν Ἰεβουσαῖον, ἑπτὰ ἔθνη πολλὰ, καὶ μεγάλα, καὶ ἰσχυρότερα ὑμῶν, καὶ παραδώσει αὐτοὺς Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ὑμῶν εἰς χεῖράς σου, καὶ πατάξεις αὐτοὺς, ἀφανισμῷ ἀφανίσεις αὐτούς. Οὐ διαθήσῃ πρὸς αὐτοὺς διαθήκην, οὐδ' οὐ μὴ ἐλεήσεις αὐτοὺς, οὐδὲ μὴ γαμβρεύσεις πρὸς αὐτούς. Τὴν θυγατέρα σου οὐ δώσεις τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ, καὶ τὴν θυγατέρα αὐτοῦ οὐ λήψῃ τῷ υἱῷ σου, ἀποστήσει γὰρ τὸν υἱόν σου ἀπ' ἐμοῦ, καὶ λατρεύσει θεοῖς ἑτέροις.» Ἀσφαλὴς οὖν ὁ νόμος. «Οὐ γὰρ συνθήσῃ,» φησὶ, «διαθήκην πρὸς αὐτούς·» ἀσύμβατον γὰρ καὶ ἀσυναφὲς τῷ ἡγιασμένῳ, τὸ βέβηλον ἔτι, τῷ πεφωτισμένῳ, τὸ ἐν ὁμίχλῃ καὶ σκότῳ, τῷ εἰσδεδεγμένῳ τὸ ἀπαράδεκτον· τῷ πρὸς ἱεράν τε καὶ θείαν εἰσφοιτῶντι σκηνὴν, τὸ ταύτης ἐξωθούμενον. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Εἶτα τί τὸ προμηθὲς τοῦ νόμου; διίστησι δὲ ἀνθ' ὅτου καὶ τοῦτο εἰσάπαν τοῦ βεβήλου τὸ καθαρὸν, κἂν εἰ ἐν καλῷ τις γένοιτο τῆς ἀρετῆς; {ΚΥΡ.} Πολὺ γὰρ δὴ λίαν τὸ δέος, ὦ τᾶν· μὴ ἄρα πως καὶ τό γε ὀρθῶς ἑστάναι δοκοῦν, τὸν ἐφ' ἃ μὴ προσῆκον εἰσδέξαιτο κλόνον καὶ παρενεχθείη τοῦ πρέποντος, ὑπό του τυχὸν ἐκβεβιασμένον, ἢ ἐρεθιζούσης ἡδονῆς, ἢ κατωθούσης εἰς τὸ πλημμελὲς, τῆς ἐνούσης τῇ φύσει πρὸς τοῦτο ῥοπῆς. Ἀπονένευκε γὰρ ἀεί πως ἐπὶ τὸ φαῦλον, καὶ θεῖος ἡμῖν ἐπιμαρτύρει λόγος· «Ἐπιμελῶς γὰρ ἔγκειται,» φησὶν, «ἡ διάνοια τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐπὶ τὰ πονηρὰ ἐκ νεότητος.» Παραθείην δ' ἂν ἐθέλοντί σοι πρὸς ἀπόδειξιν ἐναργῆ, τὰ ὅσαπερ αὐτὴν ὑπομεῖναι λόγος τὴν ἐξ Ἰακώβ. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Δίναν δή που φής· οἶμαι γὰρ ὡδί. {ΚΥΡ.} Πάνυ μὲν οὖν, ὦ Παλλάδιε· γέγραπται γὰρ οὕτως ἐν τῷ τῆς Γενέσεως βιβλίῳ· «Καὶ ἦλθεν
pass_a_gloss: ... for one might say also upon them, just as of course also upon the Jews: 'For I bear witness to them that they have zeal of God, but not according to knowledge' [Romans 10:2]. For thinking to be right-speaking and wise, the wretched have escaped their own notice both fighting the doctrines of the truth, and, overpowered by a fabricated zeal, they think to plead-together-for the glory of God, ranging themselves against those walking-straight. But the Moabites, that is, the troops of the Hellenes, nakedly and openly and without all reserve fight the divine glory. Therefore the law somehow hung a more burdensome penalty on them. Except both [are] sent away from the sacred enclosures, as profane and God-hated. PALL.: A thing then not harmless, as far as concerns defilements, to love to go even into words with certain foreign and other-minded persons. CYR.: You understand very well. Therefore the law also walls off the washed and clean and already God's own from the foulness of those, saying: [Deuteronomy 7:1–4 LXX: when the Lord your God brings you into the land... and you remove great, many, strong nations: Hittite, Girgashite, Amorite, Canaanite, Perizzite, Hivite, Jebusite, seven nations... stronger than you; the Lord will deliver them into your hands; you will strike them; with destruction you will destroy them; you shall not covenant a covenant with them, nor show them mercy, nor intermarry; not give your daughter to his son, nor take his daughter for your son; for he will turn away your son from me, and he will serve other gods.] Safe then the law: 'For you shall not make a covenant with them' [Deuteronomy 7:2]; for irreconcilable and unjoinable to the sanctified is the still-profane, to the enlightened the [thing] in mist and darkness, to the received the unreceivable, to the one entering into the holy and divine tabernacle the [thing] thrust out of it. PALL.: Then what [is] the forethought of the law? For what reason does it separate this too, the clean wholly from the profane, even if someone should be in a good [state] of virtue? CYR.: For very great is the fear, my good man: lest perhaps even what seems to stand rightly might receive a shaking toward what is not fitting and be carried aside from the proper, perhaps forced by someone, or pleasure provoking, or the inclination toward this that is in nature pushing down into fault. For it always somehow inclines toward the bad, and the divine word testifies: 'For carefully lies,' it says, 'the mind of man upon evil things from youth' [Genesis 8:21]. I would set before you, wishing it, for evident proof, as much as the account says that she from Jacob endured. PALL.: You mean Dinah, I suppose; for I think so. CYR.: Very much so, Palladius; for it is written thus in the book of Genesis: 'And came...
pass_b_english: Cyril: …of them too, just as of the Jews: ‘For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge’ (Romans 10:2). Thinking that they speak rightly and are wise, the wretches do not notice that they are fighting against the doctrines of the truth; and, mastered by a counterfeit zeal, they think that they are pleading the cause of God’s glory when they set themselves against those who walk uprightly. But the Moabites, that is, the ranks of the pagans, fight against the divine glory nakedly and openly, holding nothing back. That is why the law has hung a heavier penalty over them. Yet both are sent away from the sacred precincts as unholy and hateful to God.
Palladius: So it is no harmless thing, where defilement is concerned, to be fond of entering into talk with strangers and people of other beliefs, even if it goes no further than talk.

Cyril: You understand very well. That is why the law walls off from their foulness those who have been washed and are clean and who already belong to God, saying: ‘And it shall be, when the Lord your God brings you into the land which you are entering to inherit, and you remove great and many and strong nations from before you, the Hittite and the Girgashite and the Amorite and the Canaanite and the Perizzite and the Hivite and the Jebusite, seven nations many and great and stronger than you, and the Lord your God hands them over into your hands, and you strike them, you shall destroy them utterly. You shall not make a covenant with them, nor shall you show them mercy, nor shall you make marriages with them. You shall not give your daughter to his son, and you shall not take his daughter for your son; for he will turn your son away from me, and he will serve other gods’ (Deuteronomy 7:1–4). So the law keeps us safe. ‘For you shall not make,’ it says, ‘a covenant with them’ (Deuteronomy 7:2). For what is still unholy cannot agree or be joined with what has been made holy, nor what is in mist and darkness with what has been enlightened, nor what is rejected with what has been received, nor what is thrust out of the holy and divine tabernacle with one who enters it.
Palladius: What, then, is the law guarding against? Why does it separate the clean so entirely from the unholy, even when someone is well established in virtue?

Cyril: Because the fear is very great, my friend, that even what seems to stand upright might somehow be shaken toward what it should not and be carried away from what is fitting, forced perhaps by someone, or by pleasure stirring it, or by the leaning toward this that is in our nature pushing it down into wrongdoing. For nature always leans somehow toward what is bad, and the divine word bears witness to us: ‘For the mind of man,’ it says, ‘is intently set on evil things from his youth’ (Genesis 8:21). If you wish, I will set before you as clear proof all that the daughter of Jacob is said to have suffered.
Palladius: You mean Dinah, I suppose; at least, I take it so.
Cyril: Certainly, Palladius. For this is written in the book of Genesis: ‘And there came…

choices.english: to be fond of entering into talk ... even if it goes no further than talk
rejected: to like having dealings ... even if only in conversation
choices.why: Palladius: 'to like having dealings ... even if only in conversation' -> 'to be fond of entering into talk ... even if it goes no further than talk' (λόγους ἰέναι φιλεῖν; 'dealings' was too broad)

choices.english: what is the law guarding against
choices.why: 'what is the law's foresight here' -> 'what is the law guarding against' (τὸ προμηθές); 'stands well in virtue' -> 'is well established in virtue'

choices.english: at least, I take it so
choices.why: 'so I take it' -> 'at least, I take it so' (οἶμαι γὰρ ὡδί); 'It is written thus' -> 'For this is written' (archaism, restored γάρ)

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of De adoratione Book 14 exists to compare. Translated fresh from the Migne PG 68 Greek on 2026-10-23; the withheld earlier English was not used as a base.

apparatus.note: Migne PG 68 print; the column break may cut a sentence or a word.

Deuteronomy 7:1: Cyril's text reads ἐξαρεῖς ('you remove'); Rahlfs LXX has ἐξαρεῖ ('he removes'). The English follows Cyril. In 7:2 the quotation reads διαθήσῃ, and Cyril's repeat reads συνθήσῃ; both mean 'make a covenant'. Genesis 8:21 is quoted in the LXX form (ἐπιμελῶς ἔγκειται ἡ διάνοια); the verse number is the same in English Bibles. 'Nature always leans': the subject of ἀπονένευκε is supplied from φύσει in the clause before. 'Enlightened' (πεφωτισμένῳ) carries Cyril's usual baptismal sense; no citation. 'Pagans' renders Ἕλληνες, as in section 7. The Dinah quotation begins at the end of this section ('And there came') and finishes in section 9, where it is cited (Genesis 33:18–34:3).
restored γάρ ('For what is still unholy')
